title: Worst headache of her life
presenting_complaint: Sudden, severe occipital headache that started 2 hours ago at the gym and peaked within a minute — "like being hit with a bat". Vomited twice.
history: 48-year-old female teacher. While at the gym 2 hours ago she developed a sudden, severe occipital headache that peaked within a minute — "like being hit with a bat". She vomited twice. No loss of consciousness, no seizure, no head trauma. Past medical history: hypertension, poorly controlled, on amlodipine. Smokes. Mother died of a "brain bleed" at 52. Not on anticoagulants or antiplatelets.

findings.name: Neurological examination
findings.value: GCS 15, pupils equal and reactive, no focal neurological deficit

findings.name: Meningeal signs
findings.value: Photophobia and neck stiffness present; Kernig sign negative

findings.name: Non-contrast head CT (2 hours from onset)
findings.value: Hyperdense blood in the basal cisterns and the Sylvian fissures

findings.name: CT angiography
findings.value: 7 mm aneurysm of the anterior communicating artery

diagnosis_options.label: Subarachnoid haemorrhage from a ruptured anterior communicating artery aneurysm
diagnosis_options.explanation: Thunderclap headache peaking within a minute, vomiting, meningism and photophobia, with hyperdense blood in the basal cisterns and Sylvian fissures on non-contrast CT, plus a 7 mm anterior communicating artery aneurysm on CT angiography.

diagnosis_options.label: Migraine
diagnosis_options.explanation: Migraine does not cause blood in the basal cisterns or an aneurysm, and rarely presents with sudden peak-within-a-minute headache with meningism.

diagnosis_options.label: Bacterial meningitis
diagnosis_options.explanation: Fever is minimal and there is no infectious syndrome; the CT shows subarachnoid blood, which meningitis would not explain.

diagnosis_options.label: Hypertensive encephalopathy
diagnosis_options.explanation: Blood pressure is elevated but there is no encephalopathy (GCS 15, no focal deficit, no papilloedema) and no explanation for subarachnoid blood.

diagnosis_options.label: Reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome
diagnosis_options.explanation: Can cause thunderclap headache but would not produce subarachnoid blood in the basal cisterns with a saccular aneurysm on angiography.

management_options.label: Urgent neurosurgical / neurointerventional referral for aneurysm securing (coiling or clipping)
management_options.explanation: Essential: securing the ruptured aneurysm prevents rebleeding.

management_options.label: Oral nimodipine 60 mg every 4 hours
management_options.explanation: Essential: reduces delayed cerebral ischaemia due to vasospasm after subarachnoid haemorrhage.

management_options.label: Control systolic BP below 160 mmHg with a titratable IV agent
management_options.explanation: Essential: blood pressure control limits the risk of rebleeding while avoiding hypoperfusion.

management_options.label: Analgesia and antiemetic
management_options.explanation: Reasonable symptomatic measure; headache and vomiting are prominent but this does not treat the underlying aneurysm.

management_options.label: Lumbar puncture now
management_options.explanation: Harmful: not needed after a diagnostic CT and risks rebleed.

management_options.label: Aspirin
management_options.explanation: Harmful in an unsecured aneurysm — increases the risk of rebleeding.
